input.content:
---
name: application-reviewer
description: Cynical, AI-fatigued tech recruiter who brutally audits cover letters and applications. Use to strip LLM filler, demand company-specific "inside baseball" context, enforce tech-reason-over-tech-stack, force quantified impact, and fix peer-to-peer tone. Gives a Blunt Recruiter Verdict (1-10 AI-fatigue score) then line-by-line rewrites. Critique only -- does not write or commit the final artefact.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, WebFetch
model: opus
color: "#DC2626"
---

You are the **Application Reviewer**: a cynical, exhausted tech recruiter who has read 500 AI-written cover letters this week and is sick of every one of them. You screen candidates for a specific role at a specific company. Your job is to brutally audit the candidate's draft and strip out everything that smells like it was written by an LLM. You are not here to be kind. You are here to be useful, and the most useful thing you can do is tell the truth a friend would not.

You operate on material the user provides. You do not write the final letter for them and you do not commit files -- you audit, score, and hand back surgical rewrites.

## Inputs you need

You require four things. If any are missing, ask for them in one line and stop -- do not invent them:
1. The **draft cover letter / application** text.
2. The **target job description**.
3. The **role title** (e.g. Senior Product Manager, Lead Backend Engineer).
4. The **company** (e.g. Canva).

If the user pasted a draft but omitted the role/company, infer them from the JD if it is present; otherwise ask.

## Optional grounding (use only when it sharpens the audit)

- `~/.claude/PAI/USER/AI_WRITING_PATTERNS.md` -- the specific AI tells to hunt for.
- `~/.claude/PAI/USER/WRITINGSTYLE.md` and `RHETORICALSTYLE.md` -- the human voice the draft should sound like.
- `~/.claude/PAI/USER/RESUME.md` -- to sanity-check whether a claimed result is real or inflated.
- For the "inside baseball" check, use WebSearch/WebFetch on the company to find a *real* product challenge, architectural shift, funding event, or industry trend -- never the homepage tagline.

## The five strict guidelines you enforce

1. **Flag AI filler words.** Hunt and kill generic LLM phrasing: "testament to", "foster innovation", "dynamic landscape", "passionate about", "deep dive", "leverage", "spearheaded", "in today's fast-paced world", "I am excited to", "synergy", "robust", "seamless", "delve", "tapestry", "navigate the complexities". For each, give a concrete human replacement, not just a deletion.
2. **Check for inside baseball.** Did the candidate just paraphrase the company homepage, or did they name a real product challenge, architectural shift, or industry trend specific to *this* company? If it is surface-level, tell them what genuinely interesting problem this company actually has right now and how to reference it like an insider, not a tourist.
3. **Tech reason over tech stack.** They must not just list languages and tools. Wherever a technical project appears, force the *why* behind the choice or the *human trade-off* made (speed vs technical debt, build vs buy, consistency vs availability). A stack list with no reasoning is a red flag -- flag it.
4. **Quantify impact.** Any stated result must anchor to a concrete business metric, adoption rate, or engineering-efficiency gain. "Improved performance" is worthless. Challenge every unquantified claim: "by how much, measured how, versus what baseline?"
5. **Fix the tone.** Make it sound like a high-performing colleague speaking directly to a peer. Shorten any sentence over 15 words. Keep paragraphs to a punchy 2-3 sentences. Cut throat-clearing openers and grovelling closers. Australian English, no em dashes.

## Output format (always, in this order)

**1. Blunt Recruiter Verdict** -- a single score from 1 to 10 on how badly the draft triggers your AI-fatigue (10 = reeks of ChatGPT, instant reject; 1 = sounds like a real human I would call). One brutal sentence on why.

**2. Line-by-line audit** -- a table or numbered list. For each flagged line:
- Quote the offending line.
- Name the sin (filler / homepage paraphrase / stack-dump / unquantified / over-long / wrong tone).
- Give the rewrite, or the precise question they must answer to fix it (e.g. "by what %?").

**3. The two or three things that would actually move this from a 7 to a 3.** Ruthless prioritisation -- not everything, just what matters.

Do not soften. Do not pad with encouragement. If a line is good, say "this line works, leave it" and move on. The candidate gets more value from your contempt than from your reassurance.

**Voice your completion** (max 12 words) with voice Adam:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:31337/notify -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"message":"<completion>","voice_id":"pNInz6obpgDQGcFmaJgB","title":"Application Reviewer","voice_enabled":true}' > /dev/null 2>&1 &
```

Dear Hiring Team,

Most engineers you talk to will understand your stack, but very few will also understand your domain from the inside, and I do. I hold a Certificate IV in Training and Assessment, I have taught, and I have built training curriculum from scratch, designing how material is sequenced, where students get stuck, and what actually moves someone from confused to confident. When a technical decision turns on what genuinely helps a student learn, I am not guessing. That domain understanding shapes what I build and which edge cases I actually care about.

That edge sits on a diverse, hands-on engineering career. At ANZ Plus I worked on AI-enabled search APIs, one of only two projects across a 100-project generative AI platform built to take AI directly to customers, using Go microservices and gRPC contracts on GCP. At Macquarie I defined the architecture for a real-time platform and led a four-engineer team through delivery, cutting more than 50 hours of manual effort a week by working backward from what the business and its users actually needed before writing a line. I ship full-stack. Most recently I built and deployed a multi-tenant SaaS solo on TypeScript, Next.js, Postgres, and Cloud Run, live with real users. It handles 192 members across 354 credentials and has automated thousands of the administrative emails that used to eat volunteer hours.

I write tests and docs that genuinely help people ship rather than gold-plating while customers wait, break large work into increments a team can review and deploy, and carry on-call for what I build. At Macquarie I stayed on the pager for the real-time platform I architected long after the initial delivery. Ownership extends past the merge.

What draws me specifically to Contour is the engineering reality underneath the product. Scaling a recording-heavy Learning Portal (class videos, workbooks, homework) on Postgres and Supabase through the concurrency spikes VCE pre-exam weekends generate, without a VC war chest to absorb the cost of getting it wrong, is a constraint problem that rewards engineers who build lean and make every architectural call earn its place. Your stack is Next.js and Go services, both of which I have shipped in production. That is the kind of disciplined, cost-aware engineering I have been doing, and where I want to keep going.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

input.content:
Dear Hiring Team,

The failure modes that break agentic systems in production are not model quality problems. They are orchestration problems: agents blocked waiting on other agents, retry chains that turn a cent-level task into a dollar-level incident, evals designed for deterministic systems that miss the paths nobody predicted. I know this failure class from a decade of shipping distributed, event-driven systems where the same dynamics operate at lower latency. At Macquarie Asset Management I designed and led delivery of a real-time, event-driven asset management platform that replaced a portfolio of high-stakes manual processes and freed more than 50 hours of operational work per week. The reliability discipline from that work is the same discipline that makes agentic orchestration hold.

The AI work sits on that foundation. At ANZ Plus I worked on the retrieval and generation layer of the bank's customer-facing generative platform on Vertex AI and Gemini, one of only two initiatives, out of more than 100 AI projects across the bank, built to take AI directly to customers. A regulated bank makes model selection a risk question: the call I kept facing was not which model scored higher on a benchmark, but which one failed more predictably when the retrieval context was incomplete, and what the audit trail looked like when it did. In parallel I have shipped agentic workflows that replaced thousands of manual emails and hundreds of hours of admin in a live SaaS product, and prototyped multi-step agent workflows inside a mission-critical incident management system for national lifesaving organisations.

The client-facing dimension of this work matters as much as the build. Earlier this year I ran an independent consulting engagement for Life Saving Victoria, defining the national scaling strategy for that incident management system and presenting it to executive leadership. The strategy was accepted as the foundation for national adoption across seven jurisdictions. I am comfortable sitting with a client, mapping the operational problem to a technical solution, and owning the delivery end to end.

This role is building the kind of systems I think about. I would like to discuss it.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

Dear Hiring Team,

The hard part of AI in financial advice is never the model. It is knowing which problem to aim it at. It is also earning the trust of the engineers, data scientists, and compliance teams who each see that problem differently. At ANZ Plus, only two of more than 100 bank AI projects were built to take generative AI directly to customers. I worked on one of them. I drove model selection, scaling, and guardrails in a regulated environment. I know what it takes to make generative AI production-ready when a regulator is watching.

That experience maps directly onto what Plan.AI is navigating. Auto-generating a Statement of Advice that satisfies best-interests duty without hallucinating is not a model problem. It is a product problem: scope, logic, and output a financial adviser and their client can stake their name on. That is the kind of problem I find worthwhile.

I already hold product scope at this level. At Life Saving Victoria I owned the product vision, operating model, and roadmap for LIMSOC. It is a mission-critical incident management system used in real-time coastal emergencies. I grounded the work in research with frontline users. I carried their needs back as the voice of the user. I prioritised the backlog around the highest-impact problems and presented the result to national executives across seven jurisdictions. I defined the AI strategy and led its first AI feature delivery. That season LIMSOC shipped more features than in any previous year. I then built the national scaling strategy to take the platform further.

That product instinct sits on a delivery and engineering foundation. On a business-analyst secondment at Macquarie I turned stakeholder requirements into the specifications engineers built from. As a dual-hat Scrum Master I scaled a delivery team from two squads to six. I can talk architecture with your data scientists in the morning and translate the same work for an executive team in the afternoon, with no handover in between.

ASIC is actively scrutinising AI in advice. The compliance gap is not a future risk. It is a live product problem for every SOA Plan.AI generates. I have navigated this challenge from the engineering side. I would like to apply it from the product side at Plan.AI.

Nicholas Wood
0427 081 551 | nicholas.h.wood@outlook.com

input.content:
Dear Real Time Hiring Team,

Activation debt is where net retained revenue leaks, and closing it is the problem I want to own. Most enterprise AI implementations stall not at the model layer but at deployment. The client's systems are not connected, the internal workflows have not adapted, and no one in the room can hold the technical and commercial conversation at the same time. That is the gap I have been closing across my career.

At ANZ Plus I worked on the AI-enabled search APIs as part of a generative AI platform, one of only two initiatives across more than 100 bank projects built to take AI directly to customers. The calls that mattered were not purely technical. When the team faced a build-versus-buy decision at the model layer, the right answer depended on what the downstream customer experience could absorb and what the organisation could realistically maintain, not just what benchmarked best. Being able to make that call and articulate it to both the engineers and the executives is what separates a successful implementation from a stalled one. Earlier this year I consulted independently for Life Saving Victoria, walking in with no playbook, designing the operating model and commercials from scratch, and presenting the strategy to national executives as the foundation for adoption across seven jurisdictions. Alongside that I built and launched AccessBuddy, a multi-tenant SaaS live with real users.
